claims.text: Integrating in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction with simultaneous thermogravimetric analysis enables direct correlation of oxidation kinetics with phase evolution.
The integrated method provides insights that neither HTXRD nor TGA can achieve independently.
The starting material is as-homogenized and single-phase, with minimal oxidation or structural defects.
An integrated in situ HTXRD-TGA setup can expose a material to high-temperature oxidizing conditions while monitoring it.
The relevant temperature range extends from approximately 750°C to above 1000°C.
High-temperature oxidation can be monitored in air or a controlled oxygen atmosphere.
In situ HTXRD can identify time- and temperature-dependent oxide-phase formation and transformation during oxidation.
Spinel or chromia may be detected as oxide phases during the proposed experiment.
The evolution of oxide phases can be coordinated with simultaneous mass-change measurements from TGA.
Real-time XRD captures the emergence and transformation of crystalline oxide phases as oxidation proceeds.
TGA records the corresponding oxidation-induced mass gain.
Combining simultaneous XRD and TGA reveals the temporal relationship between mass uptake and crystalline-phase development.
The integrated method will produce a clear, time-resolved correlation between oxidation-induced weight gain and the onset or transformation of specific crystalline phases.
The integrated method provides a more comprehensive understanding of oxidation behavior and phase stability than separate TGA or HTXRD measurements.
Separate TGA and HTXRD measurements do not provide simultaneous information about mass change and phase evolution.
Signal interference or inadequate sensitivity may prevent detection of minor phase transitions.
Insufficient temporal resolution may prevent detection of rapid changes during the earliest oxidation stages.
Detection limits and overlapping diffraction peaks may complicate quantitative correlation of mass change, phase fraction, oxidation kinetics, and phase transformations.
